title: System Design Interview Framework
tagline: A seven-step structured framework for tackling any system design question — from requirements gathering to deep dives and bottleneck discussion — so you never stare blankly at the whiteboard.

sections.content:
System design interviews have no single correct answer. What interviewers evaluate is your **structured thinking**: can you break an enormous problem into tractable pieces, make reasonable trade-offs, and communicate clearly under pressure?

The seven-step framework below gives you a repeatable scaffold. It mirrors how real engineers approach large systems — from clarifying what we are building, through rough math to check feasibility, to API contracts, data models, high-level architecture, targeted deep dives, and finally a frank discussion of bottlenecks and trade-offs.

With this framework you will never lose 15 minutes building the wrong thing because you skipped requirements. You will never propose a single relational database for a billion-user social network because you did estimation first. Structure buys you credibility — and credibility buys you the job.

sections.caption: The seven steps form a funnel: broad requirements narrow progressively to a detailed design, then widen again for honest bottleneck discussion.

sections.title: Architect Before Builder
sections.content:
Imagine you are handed a blank lot and told to 'build something for a million people'. A junior engineer grabs a shovel. A senior engineer pulls out a notepad.

The notepad phase is the framework. **Step 1** (requirements) answers: is this a parking garage or a hospital? They have very different constraints. **Step 2** (estimation) answers: how many cars per hour, how many parking spaces? Without this, you might build a two-storey structure that collapses under real load.

**Step 5** (high-level design) is the architect's blueprint — walls, floors, exits — before any concrete is poured. **Step 6** (deep dive) zooms into the elevator system or HVAC: the parts that will fail in interesting ways. **Step 7** (bottlenecks) is the honest structural review: what happens if the main entrance is blocked? What is the evacuation plan?

**Step 1 — Requirements (3–5 min):** Ask clarifying questions to nail functional requirements (what the system does) and non-functional requirements (scale, latency, availability, consistency). Typical questions: 'Who are the users?', 'How many daily active users?', 'Read-heavy or write-heavy?', 'Is strong consistency required or is eventual OK?', 'What is the acceptable latency for the critical path?'

**Step 2 — Estimation (3–5 min):** Back-of-envelope math prevents architectural mistakes. Estimate QPS (queries per second), storage per day/year, and bandwidth. Common anchors: 1 million DAU × 10 requests/day ≈ 100 QPS. 1 KB per record × 100 M records ≈ 100 GB. If the number surprises you, revisit requirements.

**Step 3 — API Design (3–5 min):** Define the public interface. Use REST or gRPC notation. List endpoints, HTTP methods, path params, request body fields, and response shapes. This forces agreement on what the system actually does before drawing any boxes.

**Step 4 — Data Model (3–5 min):** Sketch entities, key fields, and relationships. Choose your database type: relational (PostgreSQL) for structured data with ACID transactions; document store (MongoDB) for flexible schemas; key-value (Redis) for caching and sessions; wide-column (Cassandra) for time-series or write-heavy workloads; search engine (Elasticsearch) for full-text search.

**Step 5 — High-Level Design (10 min):** Draw the component diagram: clients → load balancer → web servers → service layer → cache → database → CDN. Add a message queue for async workloads. Keep it at the box-and-arrow level — no implementation code here.

**Step 6 — Deep Dive (10 min):** The interviewer will guide you to one or two hot areas: newsfeed ranking, notification delivery, file chunking, consistent hashing, write-ahead log. Go deep on the hard parts: data structures, algorithms, consistency guarantees.

**Step 7 — Bottlenecks and Trade-offs (3–5 min):** Identify single points of failure. Discuss replication strategies, sharding keys, CDN placement, circuit breakers, rate limiting, and monitoring. Acknowledge trade-offs explicitly: 'We sacrifice strong consistency for availability here because…'

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: The estimation helper quantifies scale early — 10 M DAU with 50 requests each at 2 KB produces ~580 GB/day, ~212 TB/year. That immediately rules out a single-server setup. The consistent hash ring demonstrates a deep-dive concept: keys map to server nodes and adding/removing a node only remaps 1/n of keys.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Speak before you draw.** Interviewers reward communication. Before touching the whiteboard, say aloud: 'I am going to start with requirements, then do a quick estimation, then propose an API, data model, high-level design, and we can dive deeper into whichever component you care most about. Does that sound good?' This signals structured thinking in the first 30 seconds and earns you control of the conversation.

items: **Requirements first** — 5 minutes of clarifying questions prevents 30 minutes of designing the wrong system.
**Estimation** grounds the design in real numbers; if QPS is 10, a single DB is fine; if QPS is 100 K, you need sharding and caching from day one.
**API design** locks in the contract before drawing components — every box in the diagram must serve a clear API consumer.
**Data model and DB choice** is one of the highest-signal decisions: relational vs. document vs. wide-column vs. key-value each make different trade-offs.
**High-level design** stays at the box-and-arrow level — load balancer, caches, queues, workers, replicas.
**Deep dive** is where you demonstrate real expertise — consistent hashing, write-ahead logs, fanout strategies, or exactly-once delivery.

**Bottlenecks last** — acknowledge SPOFs, sharding keys, replication lag, and monitoring honestly; no real system is perfect and interviewers respect engineers who know the limits of their own designs.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of the estimation step in a system design interview?
options: To show mathematical ability.
To ground architectural decisions in real-world scale and prevent over- or under-engineering.
To calculate the exact cost of the system on AWS.
To determine the number of engineers needed to build it.
quiz.explanation: Estimation translates vague scale ('millions of users') into concrete numbers (QPS, storage TB). Those numbers directly inform whether you need sharding, caching, CDNs, and how many servers — preventing both over-engineering a small system and under-engineering a large one.

quiz.question: Why should you design the API before drawing the high-level component diagram?
options: Interviewers always evaluate API design first.
The API contract defines what each component must do, keeping the diagram grounded in real requirements.
APIs are simpler to design than component diagrams.
REST APIs eliminate the need for a data model.
quiz.explanation: The API is the contract between clients and services. Defining it first ensures every component in the diagram has a clear purpose — serving a specific API endpoint. Without it, boxes and arrows become decoration.

quiz.question: Which database type is most appropriate for write-heavy time-series data at massive scale?
options: PostgreSQL (relational)
Redis (key-value)
Cassandra (wide-column)
Elasticsearch (search engine)
quiz.explanation: Cassandra is a wide-column store designed for high write throughput and linear horizontal scaling. Its partition-by-time-bucket approach makes it the industry standard for time-series workloads (IoT, metrics, logs).

quiz.question: What does a message queue add to a high-level architecture?
options: Strong consistency between all services.
Asynchronous decoupling — producers do not wait for consumers, and bursts are absorbed.
Automatic sharding of the primary database.
Encryption of data in transit.
quiz.explanation: A message queue (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ) decouples producers from consumers. Producers write and move on; consumers process at their own pace. This absorbs traffic spikes and prevents cascading failures.

quiz.question: In the cache-aside (lazy-loading) pattern, what happens on a cache miss?
options: The request is rejected with a 503 error.
The cache fetches the data from the DB autonomously.
The application fetches the data from the DB, stores it in the cache, then returns it.
The load balancer reroutes to a backup server.
quiz.explanation: Cache-aside: the application checks the cache first. On a miss, it reads from the database, writes the result into the cache with a TTL, and returns the data. The cache is populated lazily — only on demand.

quiz.question: What problem does consistent hashing solve in distributed systems?
options: It ensures all nodes have the same data at all times.
It minimises key remapping when nodes are added or removed from the cluster.
It encrypts data with a consistent algorithm across all servers.
It guarantees ACID transactions across multiple databases.
quiz.explanation: With simple modulo hashing (key % n), adding or removing one server remaps almost all keys. Consistent hashing places servers on a virtual ring so that only the keys nearest the changed node are remapped — O(k/n) remapping instead of O(k).

quiz.question: Which step in the framework is best for discussing replication lag and single points of failure?
options: Step 1 — Requirements
Step 3 — API Design
Step 5 — High-Level Design
Step 7 — Bottlenecks and Trade-offs
quiz.explanation: Step 7 is the dedicated space for honest critique: SPOFs, replication lag, sharding limits, monitoring gaps, and acknowledged trade-offs. Raising these earlier can derail the design before it is fully established.

quiz.question: A social network has 50 M DAU each reading 20 posts per day. What is the approximate average read QPS?
quiz.explanation: 50M × 20 = 1,000M requests/day. 1,000M / 86,400 seconds ≈ 11,574 QPS. Rounding to ~11,600 QPS indicates a need for multiple web servers, caching, and read replicas — a single server cannot handle this.

quiz.question: What should you do in the first 30 seconds of a system design interview?
options: Start drawing boxes on the whiteboard immediately to show confidence.
Ask all clarifying questions about the non-functional requirements.
Announce your framework and ask if the approach sounds good.
Write out the database schema for the core entity.
quiz.explanation: Announcing your framework ('I will start with requirements, then estimation, API, data model, high-level design, deep dive, bottlenecks — does that work?') signals structured thinking, earns control of the interview, and sets the interviewer's expectations.

quiz.question: When is a message queue NOT the right solution?
options: When you need to send a welcome email after user registration.
When processing video thumbnails asynchronously.
When a user needs an immediate synchronous response (e.g. 'your balance is $50').
When absorbing write bursts before they hit the database.
quiz.explanation: Message queues are asynchronous — the producer does not wait for a response. For operations that require an immediate answer in the same request/response cycle (balance checks, authentication), synchronous calls are required.
